title: Refund Policy & Credit Load Policy
passageText:
**Refund Policy**

You should be aware of Bathworth’s refund policy for all fee-paying international students enrolled at Bathworth
University.

**General Refund for New Students**
A general refund may be given if written notice of withdrawal from units or intermission from a course of study is
received by the University.

**Semester 1 and 2**
- Up to and on the official starting date of the semester: 90% refund of the course fee.
- After the official starting date of a semester and up to and including the HECS census date: 50% refund of the course fee.
- When a student withdraws or discontinues from a unit or course of study after the HECS census date for the semester: No refund shall be given.

**Semester – Summer**
- Withdrawal from units up to and including 13 December: 90% refund.
- After 13 December: No refund shall be given.

**Full Refund**
A full refund may be given in special circumstances. Such circumstances should be beyond the control of the student.

**The following reasons are grounds to apply for a full refund:**
- A student is refused a student visa.
- An offer is withdrawn or an enrolment terminated because the University is unable to provide the course of study.
- A student withdraws from a unit on the advice of a Faculty Course Adviser and does not enroll in a replacement unit (the signature of the Faculty is needed).
- The University changes or is unable to offer units such that a student is prevented from completing the unit/s.
- A student is unable to fulfill the requirements of an offer.
- A student withdraws from a unit and enrolls in a replacement unit in the same semester.

Executive discretion may be exercised for applications which do not comply with the above provisions but for which
extraordinary circumstances may exist. Application for a refund in special circumstances must be made in writing and
sent to the Executive Director. Proof of payment and validation of the reasons for applying for a refund will be required.

**Methods of Refund**
- Refunds will be made in Australian dollars only, by cheque.
- Refunds in the form of the transfer of fees to another institution will not be made directly to a student. The student
  must provide evidence of acceptance into that institution before the approved refund will be transferred.

**Bathworth University Credit Load Policy**

Dear Student,

Thank you for your inquiry regarding the maximum and minimum number of courses you are allowed to enroll in at
Bathworth. Without knowing your academic record in detail, I can, at least, inform you of our credit load policies.

1. Our system of course minimums and maximums is based on the credit system. The credit system is a measure of the
   number of hours both within a class and outside of a class that a student would need to devote to a particular course.
   At Bathworth, one semester credit is equal to 32 class hours and 60 hours of study outside the class.
2. Recognizing that many of Bathworth’s students are also employed, the university recognizes 9 credits for
   undergraduates (normally 3 classes), and 6 credits for graduates as a standard full-time course load per semester.
3. The maximum credit load is 12 semester credits for undergraduate and 9 semester credits for graduate students.
4. Requests by students to exceed those limits may be approved by the Academic Dean, or may be allowed on a case-by-case basis.
   - Undergraduate students may qualify for a credit overload if they have maintained a cumulative grade point average
     of at least 2.5 for 20 credits.
   - Graduate students must have at least a 3.25 grade point average for 12 credits while enrolled at Bathworth.
5. In some cases, at the discretion of the Academic Dean, you may be allowed to take up to 20 credits if your grade point
   average is at least 3.0, and graduate students who maintain a 3.4 GPA may be given approval to take up to 12 credits.
6. This permission to exceed the load, however, is extended to a student for only one term, and is subject to review as
   the student’s circumstances change.
7. International students must attend on a full-time maximum-load basis (9 credits for undergraduates and 6 credits for
   graduates) as defined by the Immigration Authorities to maintain “active” status with the immigration authorities. All
   other credit load policies remain the same for international students.

I hope this is helpful for you in making a decision.

With regards,
Amy Fisher
Assistant to the Academic Dean

title: Red List of Threatened Species
passageText:
**Red List of Threatened Species Reveals Global Extinction Crisis**

**A**
The Earth’s most critically endangered animals and plants have been disappearing very rapidly since 1996, the world’s
largest international conservation organisation reported today.
- One in four mammal species and one in eight species of birds are facing a high risk of extinction in the near future,
  in almost all cases because of human activities.
- The total number of threatened animal species has increased from 5,205 to 5,435.
- The 2000 IUCN Red List of Threatened Species is released once every four years by the IUCN–The World Conservation Union.
- The Red List uses scientific criteria to classify species into one of eight categories: Extinct, Extinct in the Wild,
  Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Lower Risk, Data Deficient, and Not Evaluated.
- A species is classed as threatened if it falls in the Critically Endangered, Endangered, or Vulnerable categories.

**B**
“The fact that the number of critically endangered species has increased–mammals from 169 to 180; birds from 168 to
182–was a jolting surprise,” says Maritta von Bieberstein Koch-Weser, the IUCN’s director general.
- Primates such as apes and monkeys showed the greatest increase in the number of threatened mammals–from 96 to 116 species.
- Many changes were caused by increased habitat loss and hunting, particularly the bushmeat trade.
- The number of Critically Endangered primates increased from 13 to 19.
- Endangered primates number 46 today, up from 29 four years ago.

**C**
Russell Mittermeier, president of Conservation International, says, “The Red List is solid documentation of the global
extinction crisis.”
- Human and financial resources must be mobilised at between 10 and 100 times the current level to address this crisis.

**D**
- Indonesia, India, Brazil, and China are among the countries with the most threatened mammals and birds.
- Plant species are declining rapidly in South and Central America, Central and West Africa, and Southeast Asia.
- Habitat loss and degradation affect:
  - 89% of all threatened birds,
  - 83% of mammals,
  - 91% of threatened plants.
- Habitats with the highest number of threatened mammals and birds are lowland and mountain tropical rainforests.

**E**
Freshwater habitats are “extremely vulnerable” with many threatened fish, reptile, amphibian, and invertebrate species.
- Freshwater turtles went from 10 to 24 Critically Endangered species in the past four years.
- Hunting of these species is unregulated and unmanaged, with harvest levels far too high for sustainability.
- River-dwelling species face threats from water development projects and habitat changes.
- Lake-dwelling species are threatened by introduced species.

**F**
BirdLife International produced the global status analysis that forms a major component of the Red List.
- Albatrosses and petrels increased from 32 to 55 threatened species.
- Threatened penguin species doubled from five to 10.
- BirdLife International has started an international campaign titled, “Save the albatross: keeping the world’s seabirds
  off the hook.”
- The Philippines has lost 97% of its original vegetation and has more Critically Endangered birds than any other country.

**G**
The IUCN Red List includes 5,611 species of threatened plants, many of which are trees.
- One-third of the plant species in North America are threatened.
- In the last 500 years, human activity has forced 816 species to extinction or extinction in the wild.
- Approximately 25% of reptiles, 20% of amphibians, and 30% of fishes assessed are listed as threatened.

**H**
The Red List provides information on:
- Species range, population trends, main habitats, major threats, and conservation measures.
- Insight into the processes driving extinction.
- The release of the 2000 Red List comes a week before the second World Conservation Congress in Amman, Jordan,
  where members of the IUCN will meet to define global conservation policy for the next four years.

title: Interlibrary Loan Service & Migranal
passageText:
**Interlibrary Loan Service**

The Interlibrary Loan Service allows you to find books and journals that the library may not have at present but other
libraries do have. The library can borrow books or journals from other libraries on your behalf. We strive to make your
requests successful, so to help us to do so please pay attention to the following directions.

**Please make sure the following procedures are followed:**
- Clearly write the name of the book or journal, date and/or volume, and author on the pink sheet of paper titled
  Interlibrary Request Form.
- Do not use any quotes or abbreviations for repeated information.
- Write each request on a separate pink sheet.
- Include your full name, student number, and telephone number on each of the slips.

**Important Notes:**
- Allow for at least 10 working days for the material to come.
- The library will hold located resources for up to one week.
- There are no repeat requests if you happen to arrive at the library later than one week for your requests.
- It is your responsibility to check whether the materials have come in.
- The library can only track items that are no more than 10 years old.
- Fines for overdue requested material are the same as for any material borrowed from the library.

If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to ask Ms. Friedman or Betty Shipley at the information desk.

**Patient Information about Migranal**

**What does Migranal nasal spray do?**
Migranal is used to treat an active migraine headache. It is used by patients who do not get headache relief from other
pain relievers. It is not intended to prevent a headache before it occurs. Do not use it to treat common tension
headaches.

**What should my health care professional know before I use Migranal?**
The health care professional needs to know if you have any of these conditions:
- Chest pain or difficulty in breathing.
- Heart or blood vessel disease.
- High blood pressure.
- Risk factors for heart disease such as smoking and high cholesterol.
- Pregnancy or attempted pregnancy.
- Breast-feeding.

**How should I use this medicine?**
- Prepare your nasal sprayer only when you are ready to use it (at the first sign of a migraine headache).
- Do not prepare it ahead of time as it becomes unstable in 8 hours and must be discarded.
- The dose is one spray in each nostril, with the dose repeated in 15 minutes if needed.
- Each ampule contains one complete dose (4 sprays).
- Do not use more than 4 total sprays to treat a migraine headache, and use it only when you need it.
- Do not use extra doses.

**What other medicines can interact with dihydroergotamine?**
Migranal can interact with:
- Any other drug that also causes drowsiness.
- Several other drugs related to treating other diseases.

Tell your prescriber about all other medicines you are taking and if you are a frequent user of drinks with caffeine or
alcohol, if you smoke, or if you use illegal drugs. These may affect the way your medicine works.

**What side effects may I notice from receiving Migranal?**
**Side effects to report to your prescriber as soon as possible:**
- Blisters on the hands or feet.
- Muscle pain or cramps.
- Pain, tightness, or discomfort in the chest.
- Palpitations or changes in heart rate.
- Swelling or itching.
- Weakness in the legs.

Check with your prescriber if you get more frequent or severe headaches after you start using Migranal. Do not use more
than prescribed.

**Side effects that usually do not require medical attention:**
- Cold hands or feet.
- Mild dizziness or drowsiness.
- Nasal congestion.

**What do I need to watch for while I receive Migranal?**
- Migranal works best when you take it at the first sign of a headache.
- Lie down in a quiet, dark room after a dose until you feel better.
- Alcohol can make headaches worse or bring on a new headache.
- Smoking can increase the side effects of Migranal.

title: Grounds of Keele University & Services
passageText:
**Introduction to the Grounds of Keele University**

Keele University is situated in 600 acres of landscaped grounds to the west of the Potteries conurbation in North
Staffordshire. These well-wooded grounds with their lakes, streams, and formal flower beds support a wealth of wildlife.
The surrounding countryside of the Staffordshire/Shropshire/Cheshire borders is also a rich area for the naturalist and
rambler, while the majestic gritstone moorland of North Staffordshire and the limestone dales of Derbyshire and
northeast Staffordshire are not far away.

**Key Features of the Grounds:**
- Of the 600 acres, some 300 are leased out as Home Farm.
- About half of the remainder is woodland, while the rest comprises the campus buildings and sports fields.
- The landscape owes much to Ralph Sneyd (1793–1870), who began planting on a grand scale in 1830 after inheriting
  the estate from his father.

Throughout the period of its construction, the university has been careful to preserve as many mature trees as possible
and to restrict the height of buildings to maintain the feeling of living and working in a landscape. The university has a
continuing programme of landscaping, and many ornamental trees have been planted. Keele campus is, then, one of the
most picturesque and tranquil in the country, yet is only a short distance from the Potteries and the M6 motorway.

**Flora and Fauna:**
- The artificial landscape has rich flora and fauna, with:
  - More than 110 species of birds.
  - 120 species of flowering plants.
  - Over 60 species of trees.
  - 24 species of butterflies.
  - 380 species of moths.
  - 100 species of beetles.
  - 100 species of flies.
- Although there is little of great rarity, the wide variety of common species and a good network of paths make Keele an
  ideal place to visit for the casual observer, as well as for both the novice and the more experienced naturalist.

**Keele University Services For Students**

**A. English Language Unit (ELU):**
- Provides English-language tuition and support for international students.
- A small unit offering a supportive and friendly study environment.
- Many overseas students make the ELU their base for studying and making friends.

**B. Residential Support:**
- Offers information, advice, and assistance on residential problems, security concerns, and welfare issues for
  undergraduate and postgraduate students.

**C. Financial Advice:**
- Provides information and help with applications for money advice, student loans, access funds, and hardship funds.
- The Independent Advice Unit in the Students’ Union also offers advice on student finance.

**D. Counselling Service:**
- Offers help with personal, emotional, and academic issues.
- Counselling is on a one-to-one basis and is confidential.
- Both male and female counsellors are available.

**E. Exchange and Visiting Student Programmes:**
- Responsible for the administration and financial management of all exchange and visiting student programmes.
- Acts as a reference and coordinating centre for Keele students wishing to study abroad.
- Handles students studying at Keele on the Study Abroad Scheme from non-partner universities.

**F. Independent Advice Centre:**
- Offers free, confidential, and impartial advice to all students and staff.
- Part of the Students’ Union and funded by its resources.
- Stocks comprehensive information, including electronic systems and leaflets.

**G. Careers Information Room:**
- Stocks a wide range of information covering occupations, postgraduate study, funding, employment in the UK and
  overseas, and career planning.
- Provides handouts on CV writing, vacation work, and more.
- Offers alternative formats for handouts, including large print, Braille, and disk.
- Contains reports of careers staff visits to various employers.

title: Zeus' Temple Holds Secrets
passageText:
**Zeus’ Temple Holds Secrets of Ancient Games**

Athens already is preparing for the summer games of 2004. But today’s games offer a far different spectacle from the
contests of ancient Greece, where naked young men with oiled bodies raced and wrestled and boxed to honor their
gods. Those great Panhellenic events began more than 2,700 years ago, first in Olympia and later at Delphi, Isthmia, and
Nemea. At Nemea, where the games began in 573 B.C., a Berkeley archaeologist has been patiently reconstructing a site
whose legends helped inspire the modern Olympics.

**Stephen G. Miller’s Work at Nemea:**
- Miller, a professor of classics at the University of California at Berkeley, has been excavating the site every summer
  since 1973.
- His work involves analyzing artifacts, dating ancient rock strata, and assembling broken pottery shards.
- He also relives the events he studies by participating in re-enactments of the ancient Nemean games.

**Modern Re-enactments:**
- Large crowds have flocked to the ancient Nemean stadium (capacity 40,000) to watch modern re-enactments.
- Seven hundred runners from 45 nations, barefoot and clad in white tunics, raced around the reborn stadium in groups
  of 12.
- Winners were crowned with wreaths of wild celery, just as they were in antiquity.

**Key Discoveries at Nemea:**
- Limestone columns that once stood around the Temple of Zeus have been reassembled.
- A great altar to Zeus, where athletes performed sacrifices and swore oaths, was discovered east of the temple.
- Evidence of a hippodrome for horse races was found, including faint wheel marks indicating chariot races.

**The Reservoir and Locker Room:**
- In 1997, Miller’s team discovered a deep rock-walled pit, which they concluded was a reservoir for watering horses.
- Eight months later, they uncovered an ancient chamber (apodyterion) that served as a locker room for athletes.
- Athletes would anoint themselves with olive oil in the locker room before walking 120 feet through a vaulted entrance
  tunnel (krypte esodos) into the stadium.

**Artifacts and Legends:**
- A wine jug, drinking mugs, coins, and a crude figure of a centaur were found in the reservoir.
- The local red wine served in Nemean taverns today is called the Blood of Hercules, honoring the hero who strangled
  the ferocious Nemean lion.
- A tiny bronze figurine of an infant named Opheltes, whose fate inspired the first Nemean games, was unearthed.

**The Legend of Opheltes:**
- Opheltes was the son of Lykourgos and Eurydike, who were warned by the Oracle at Delphi that their child must not
  touch the ground until he learned to walk.
- A Nemean slave woman placed the child on a bed of wild celery while offering drink to seven warrior heroes passing
  through Nemea.
- A serpent killed the infant, and the warriors renamed him Archemoros (the “Beginner-of-Doom”) and held the first
  Nemean games in his honor.
- Winners of those games were crowned with wreaths of wild celery, as they are in modern re-enactments.

**Challenges and Future Plans:**
- Each excavation season at Nemea costs at least $150,000, funded entirely by private sources.
- Miller lectures to the public and seeks contributions to support the project.
- The team continues to organize and classify their finds while planning for future digs.

**Conclusion:**
Miller’s work at Nemea sheds light on the complex interplay of religion and athletics in ancient Greece, linking
archaeological discoveries to the legends that inspired the modern Olympic Games.

title: Great Barrier Island Transport
passageText:
**Walking**

- There are ten walking tracks that go through native forest or around beaches.
- Hiking times and degree of difficulty vary from 30 minutes (very easy) to five hours (quite demanding).
- Views are stunning.

**Mountain Biking**

- Recent track development by the Department of Conservation makes biking exciting on Great Barrier.
- It is New Zealand law to wear a helmet when riding.
- Watch out for walkers as they share tracks.

**Surfing and Swimming**

- There are several famous surf beaches with big waves.
- Inland, there are hot springs.
- Bring plenty of sunscreen because the UV rays are extremely dangerous.
  - Burn times in mid-summer are as low as ten minutes.
  - You still burn in the water.

**Kayaking and Diving**

- Two hire companies operate on Great Barrier for all the gear you need.
- Kayaking is done on the sheltered western side of the island.
- Snorkeling and scuba diving are popular everywhere.
- The wreck of the Wiltshire, off the south coast, provides extra interest.

**Fishing and a Seafood Festival**

- Eating seafood is a must.
  - Indulge in fish caught by locals.
  - Try your luck at some popular fishing spots.
- January sees the Mussel Festival.
  - Shellfish is cooked up in every way imaginable.
  - Accompanied by musical performances.

**Learning About Local History**

- The hardwood forests on Great Barrier Island were exploited for over 100 years by loggers.
- Walking around, you will see ruins from this industry.
- Most trees are protected these days.
- There are some old wooden houses from the 19th century that make for excellent photographs.

**Mature-Aged Students**

**A. Changing Trends:**
- A generation ago, few tertiary students began their studies over the age of 21.
- Today, large numbers of mature-aged students are studying both online and on campus.
- In some countries, such as China, university study remains primarily for the young.

**B. Reasons for the Rise:**
- Universities have changed entry requirements as more courses have become fee-paying.
- The concept of a job for life is outdated; retraining for longer working lives is essential.
- General expansion of the education sector to meet workforce demands.

- Advantages:
  - Higher salary potential after study.

- Challenges:

- Mature-aged students juggle work, family, and other commitments.

**F. Drop-Outs:**
- Discouraged drop-outs feel they failed twice, causing anxiety.
- Fortunately, completion rates for mature-aged students are high.

**G. Success Stories:**
- Completing studies requires courage, determination, and sacrifice.
- Despite difficulties, many mature-aged students succeed worldwide.

title: The Humble Banana
passageText:
**The Humble Banana**

As the world’s most eaten fruit, it is hard to believe that the banana has only become widely available in the last one
hundred years. Nor can most people imagine a world without bananas. However, disease is threatening the existence of
popular varieties, and while the banana itself is unlikely to die out, what consumers call a banana could change
dramatically since new disease-resistant strains may differ in taste, texture, size, and colour from fruit currently on offer.

**History**

- Native to tropical South and Southeast Asia.
- First cultivated in today’s Papua New Guinea around 10,000 years ago.
- Spread to Madagascar, Africa, and the Islamic world before reaching Europe in the 15th century.
- The word ‘banana’ entered English via Portuguese from Wolof, a West African language.
- Plantation-grown bananas from Central America flooded the global market by the early 20th century.

**Botanical Data**

- Most modern edible bananas come from Musa acuminata, Musa balbisiana, or their hybrids.
- Two common varieties:
  - Cavendish: Larger and more curved.
  - Lady Finger: Smaller and straighter.
- Bananas are herbs, not trees, and can grow over seven metres (24 ft).
- The stem dies after fruiting, and the plant regenerates from an underground corm.
- Domesticated bananas no longer have seeds and are propagated through corm transplantation or tissue culture.

**Uses and Benefits**

- Bananas grow year-round, making them a vital crop.
- Easy to eat (just peel) and transport (no packaging needed).
- Edible parts: Fruit, skin, heart, and stem.
- Nutritional benefits:
  - One 100-gram banana provides:
    - 371 kilojoules (89 kcal) of energy.
    - 28% of daily Vitamin B6.
    - 15% of daily Vitamin C.
    - 8% of daily potassium.
  - Lowers the risk of breast, bowel, or liver cancer.
  - Increases dopamine levels, improving mood.
- Other uses:
  - Leaves used as plates or food containers in Asia.
  - Banana fibre used for cloth and paper.
  - Skins used to clean polluted rivers due to high absorption of heavy metals.
- Cultural significance:
  - Tamils consider bananas one of three holy fruits.
  - Buddhists offer bananas to the Buddha.
  - Moslems consume bananas in large quantities during Ramadan.

**Threats to Bananas**

- **Gros Michel:**
  - Dominated the market between 1820 and 1950.
  - Nearly wiped out by Panama disease.
- **Cavendish:**
  - Replaced Gros Michel but is genetically identical, making it vulnerable to disease.
  - Threatened by Tropical Race 4 (TR4), a mutation of Panama disease.
- **Black Sigatoka:**
  - Reduced Ugandan banana crops by 40% in the 1970s.
  - Treatment costs $1000 per hectare annually and contaminates soil and water.
- **Banana Xanthomonas Wilt:**
  - Hit East Africa in 2010, causing $500 million in losses for Uganda.
  - Thousands of farmers abandoned bananas, leading to financial hardship and poorer diets.
- **Solutions:**
  - Genetic modification: Adding sweet pepper genes to bananas for disease resistance.
  - Domestication of disease-free wild bananas.

**Conclusion**

Human civilization has a long and critical relationship with bananas. If this is to continue, it may be time to reconsider
what a banana is. Supermarkets may no longer stock big sweet yellow cultivars but instead offer tiny purple, pink, red,
or green-and-white striped bananas that currently exist in the depths of the forest.

title: The Young Person's Railcard & Train Travel Information
passageText:
**The Young Person’s Railcard**

A Young Person’s Railcard gives young people the opportunity to purchase discounted rail tickets across Britain.
Just imagine where it could take you – to festivals, to see distant friends, or to London for a weekend break.

**Who Can Apply?**

- Anybody between 16 and 25 can apply.
- Proof of age is required (birth certificate, driving licence, passport, or medical card).
- Mature students over 25 in full-time education can also apply.
  - Full-time education: Over 15 hours per week for at least 20 weeks a year.
  - Application form must be signed by a headteacher, tutor, or head of department.
  - One photo must be officially stamped.
- Application requirements:
  - Completed form from the leaflet.
  - £28 fee.
  - Two passport-sized photos.
  - Proof of eligibility.
- Submit applications at major railway stations, rail-appointed travel agents, or authorised student travel offices.

**Using Your Railcard**

- Valid at any time: Weekends, Bank Holidays, or weekdays.
- Minimum fares apply before 10 am Monday to Friday (except July and August).
  - For details, ask at your local station or rail-appointed travel agent.

**Conditions**

- Railcards without a signature are invalid.
- Railcards and discounted tickets are non-transferable.
- Full fare applies if:
  - No valid ticket is produced during inspection.
  - No purchase facilities were available at the station where the journey began.
- Reduced rate tickets are not valid for:
  - First-class travel.
  - Eurostar links to France and Belgium.

**Train Travel Information**

We offer several distinct options for you to choose the ticket that suits you best.

**Ticket Types and Discounts**

- **Standard Returns:** 20% discount; return within 60 days of the outward trip.
- **Same Day Returns:** 25% discount; ticket cannot be altered or refunded.
- **Children:** 40% discount for ages 4 to 11.
- **Students:** 25% discount; student card must be shown.
- **Senior Citizens:** 25% discount; seniors card must be shown.
- **Groups (10-25 people):** 15% discount on each section of the trip.
- **Globe-Trotter Tickets:** Discounts vary (Railpass, Tourist Card, Econopass).
  - Only one discount may apply to each fare.

**Changes and Refunds**

- Tickets may be refunded up to 5 minutes before departure for a 15% charge.
- Journeys may be changed to another day for a 10% charge.
  - Not applicable to same day returns.
- Same day travel changes:
  - Tickets can be changed once without charge for a journey on the same day.

**Information for Travellers**

- Check dates and times on your ticket when purchasing.
- Ticket control and platform access close 2 minutes before departure.
- Luggage allowance:
  - One suitcase and one item of hand luggage per traveller.
  - 15 kg of luggage can be checked in up to 30 minutes before departure at no extra charge.
- For train charters or reservations for over 25 passengers, contact the Sales Department.

**Our Timetable Guarantee**

- If your train arrives more than 5 minutes late at your destination, you will receive a full refund.
  - Refunds apply only if the delay is caused by our company.

title: Professional Credentials & Business Presentations
passageText:
**Professional Credentials: Advice for Immigrants**

As an immigrant to North America, you will need to ensure that employers and organisations such as colleges and
universities properly recognise your international credentials.

**Key Points to Consider**

- Credentials may include:
  - Trade certificates.
  - Educational qualifications (degrees or diplomas).
- Challenges:
  - Hiring personnel often lack training in evaluating international academic backgrounds.
  - 60% of jobs require formal education, but 40% of HR staff may not recognise foreign documents.
- Salary considerations:
  - Immigrants may start with lower salaries compared to North American-trained individuals.
  - Seek companies that understand your situation or can guide you to obtain North American qualifications.

**Apprenticeship Training**

- Hands-on program with:
  - 10% classroom training at community colleges.
  - 90% on-the-job training.
- Duration: Up to 5 years.
- Benefits:
  - Earn income during training.
  - Potential for long-term job security.
  - May count toward college or university credits.

**Credential Translation and Assessment**

- Translate your documents if earned outside North America.
- Use an accredited assessment service for job applications.
- Include the evaluation report with your cover letter.
- Tips:
  - Provide the report early in the application process.
  - Ensure employers screen you ‘in’ rather than ‘out’.

**Diversity in the Workforce**

- Establishing yourself in North America is challenging.
- Companies are improving diversity and integrating immigrants into the workforce.

**How to Prepare for a Presentation**

The first time your boss suggests that you formally present something to your department or a client, your reaction may
be to panic. But remember that being asked to present is a compliment.

**Steps to Prepare**

1. **Define Your Big Idea:**
   - Condense your topic into one sentence.
   - Decide what you want your audience to remember.
2. **Develop Supporting Points:**
   - Identify three main points to support your topic.
   - Use stories to illustrate each point.
3. **Make It Visual:**
   - Use props to make your talk engaging.
   - Example: Hold a toy phone when discussing customer service.
4. **Start Dynamically:**
   - Avoid generic openings like ‘Thank you for inviting me.’
   - Use anecdotes or an enthusiastic introduction to capture attention.
5. **Plan Your Ending:**
   - Finish memorably with a game or humorous story.
   - Ensure your audience leaves with a positive impression.
6. **Practice:**
   - Avoid memorising or reading word-for-word.
   - Practise your introduction and conclusion for confidence.

By following these steps, you can deliver a presentation that is engaging, memorable, and effective.

title: The Birdmen
passageText:
**The Birdmen**

**Will people finally be able to fly long distances without a plane?**

John Andres investigates

People have dreamt of flying since written history began. In the 1400s, Leonardo da Vinci drew detailed plans for human
flying machines. You might have thought the invention of mechanised flight would have put an end to such ideas. Far
from it. For many enthusiasts, the ultimate flight fantasy is the jet pack, a small piece of equipment on your back which
enables you to climb vertically into the air and fly forwards, backwards, and turn.

**Jet Packs**

- Eric Scott, a Hollywood stuntman for a decade, has used jet packs over 600 times.
- Now works for an energy-drink company, advertising Go Fast drinks while flying.
- Current jet packs work for about 30 seconds, but designs for 20-minute flights are in progress.

**Paramotoring**

- Combines a paragliding parachute with a small engine and propeller.
- Chris Clarke, a paramotorist for five years, notes:
  - Comparable in expense to driving a petrol-powered car.
  - Ill-suited for commuting due to difficulty taking off in strong winds.
- Patrick Vandenbulcke’s experience:
  - Noticed burning during a flight; the exhaust pipe had moved, melting the harness.
  - Warns against self-teaching; recommends professional training (costs over £1,000).
  - Equipment costs a few thousand pounds; secondhand options available.

**Yves Rossy: The Birdman**

- Born in 1959 in Switzerland.
- Career:
  - Air force pilot (ages 20-28).
  - Commercial airline pilot (1988-2000).
- Transitioned to becoming the first jet-powered flying man.

**Achievements**

- In May 2008, Rossy:
  - Stepped out of an aircraft at 3,000 metres.
  - Soared and dived at over 290 kph, reaching 300 kph.
  - Used four jet turbines attached to aerodynamic carbon foldable wings.
  - Released a parachute to land safely.
- Wings manufactured by JCT Composites:
  - Initially approached Jet-Kit, but their wings were not rigid enough.
  - JCT Composites’ wings enabled stable horizontal flight.

**Future Plans**

- Ambition: Fly down the Grand Canyon.
- Challenges:
  - Requires bigger, more powerful jets.
  - Current engines allow climbing but need more thrust for sustained flight.
- Physical demands:
  - Comparable to riding a motorbike.
  - Requires focus on relaxing in the air to avoid swinging.

**Conclusion**

Rossy’s achievements inspire hope for future personal flight. However, it is likely to remain an expensive hobby for most
people.

title: School Attendance & Holiday Apartments
passageText:
**Is Your Child at School Today?**

**School Attendance Information for Parents/Carers**

**Introduction**

Receiving a good full-time education will give your child the best possible start in life. Attending school regularly and
punctually is essential if children are to make the most of the opportunities available to them. The law says that parents
must ensure that their child regularly attends the school where he/she is registered.

**What You Can Do to Help**

- Make sure your child arrives at school on time.
  - Encourages good timekeeping habits.
  - Reduces classroom disruption.
  - Note: Late arrivals after the register has closed without a good reason will be recorded as ‘unauthorised’ absences.
- Inform the school of absences:
  - Notify the school on the first morning of absence.
  - Follow the school’s attendance policy for reporting absences.
- Contact the school if your child has difficulties attending.
  - Addressing issues early can resolve problems quickly.

**Authorised and Unauthorised Absence**

- **Authorised Absences:**
  - Sickness.
  - Unavoidable medical or dental appointments (preferably after school or during holidays).
  - Interviews with prospective employers or colleges.
  - Exceptional family circumstances (e.g., bereavement).
  - Days of religious observance.
- **Unauthorised Absences:**
  - Shopping during school hours.
  - Day trips.
  - Unapproved holidays.
  - Birthdays.
  - Looking after siblings or ill relatives.

**Holiday Apartments to Let**

**A:**
- Sleeps 2-3.
- One-bedroom apartment with uninterrupted sea views.
- Located in a well-established complex with leisure facilities and a supermarket.
- On the edge of town, close to cafés and restaurants.
- On-street parking generally available.

**B:**

- Five minutes’ walk from the sea.
- Private parking in front of the building.
- Located in a quiet village with a market, banks, cafés, and restaurants.
- Championship golf courses within walking distance.

**C:**

- One-bedroom cottage with a large terrace offering river and mountain views.
- Peaceful location in a picturesque village.
- Less than ten minutes’ drive from the coast and town amenities.
- Owners live nearby and are happy to assist.

**D:**
- Sleeps 2-5.
- Two-bedroom apartment in a complex with a pool and views of the national park.

- Town offers shops and excellent sports facilities.
- Superb local golf courses within easy reach.

**E:**
- Sleeps 2-4.
- Modern one-bedroom first-floor apartment in a house.
- Owners reside on the ground floor.
- Close to town amenities, including a supermarket, bank, cafés, and restaurants.
- Ferry to the island beach is 100 m away.

title: The Zebras' Long Walk
passageText:
**The Zebras’ Long Walk Across Africa**

James Gifford investigates some interesting new research into migration patterns of zebras living in Botswana in southern Africa.

**A**

- For any animal to travel over 270 km in Botswana partly across the sand and low bush terrain of the Kalahari Desert is a remarkable achievement.
- Zebras complete this journey in 11 days without any obvious motivation.
- Their journey involves an exhausting round-trip of 588 km between the Makgadikgadi salt pan area and the Okavango river.
- This migration is second only to the great trek undertaken by the zebra herds in the Serengeti National Park.
- Until recently, this migration was completely unheard of.

**B**

- Hattie Bartlam, a researcher, discovered this migration while tracking zebra groups (harems) by the Okavango river for her PhD.
- Each harem consists of:
  - A stallion.
  - Seven or eight mares with juvenile foals.
- There is no loyalty between zebras beyond this social group, though harems often gather into herds.
- Hattie planned to compare the small-scale movement patterns of 11 different zebra herds in the area.

**C**

- In December, during the annual rains, Hattie discovered six harems 270 km away on the edge of the Makgadikgadi.
- The Makgadikgadi is a huge mineral-rich area where salt has collected over the years as water evaporates in the heat.
- By May, five of those harems returned to the Okavango.
- Questions raised:
  - Why were the zebras drawn eastwards to the salt pans despite a plentiful supply of food and water?
  - Why did six groups travel so far while the other five remained by the Okavango?

**D**

- This discovery created a buzz in the research community.
- A century ago, Botswana’s zebra and wildebeest herds migrated due to competition for grass.
- Migration tracks included the route from the Okavango to Makgadikgadi.
- In the late 1960s, fences were erected to prevent disease spread between wildlife and domestic cattle.
  - These fences made the journey 200 km longer, an impossible distance due to lack of water.
- The fences were removed in 2004, but there is still dangerously little drinking water to support the zebras’ return journey.

**E**

- Zebras can live up to 20 years, meaning migration skipped at least one generation during the 40 years the fences were up.
- It is assumed that young zebras learn migratory behaviour from their parents.
- Questions raised:
  - How did the latest generation learn when and where to go?
  - Did they follow another species, such as elephants?

**F**

- Hattie’s data suggests three zebra populations with different behaviours:
  1. **Group One:**
     - Spend the entire year by the Okavango river.
  2. **Group Two:**
     - 15,000-20,000 strong.
     - Divide their time between the Makgadikgadi salt pans and the Boteti River.
     - Struggle to find water in the Boteti area during the dry season.
     - Reward: Juicy grass around the Makgadikgadi after the rains.
  3. **Group Three:**
     - Numbers are modest but unknown.
     - Undertake the extraordinary journey between the Okavango and the salt pans.
     - Enjoy the best of both worlds but pay the price of an extraordinary journey.

**G**

- Zebras, though relatively abundant, are vital to the food chain.
- Understanding their migration helps interpret the movements of their predators.
- Hattie’s research highlights the impact of fences on migratory animals.
- Hattie’s interest in zebras:
  - Easier to get funding to study exciting animals like lions.
  - Believes herbivores like zebras are key to understanding ecosystems.
- The scientific community benefits from researchers like Hattie who take the hard option.

title: Sustainable School Travel & Flu Facts
passageText:
**Sustainable School Travel Strategy**

- Over the last 20 years, the number of children being driven to school in England has doubled.
- National data suggests:
  - One in five cars on the road at 8.50 am is engaged in the school run.
  - Children are exposed to up to 3.9 times more pollution in a car standing in traffic than when walking or cycling to school.
- Benefits of reducing cars around schools:
  - Safer school environments.
  - Improved health and environmental outcomes.
  - Teachers note that children engaging in active travel arrive at school more alert and ready to learn.

**County Council’s Commitment**

- The County Council supports and promotes sustainable school travel.
- Annual data collection on how pupils travel to school.
- Achievements:
  - Reduced the number of cars on the daily school run by an average of 1% annually over the last three years.
  - Equivalent to removing approximately 175 cars from the road each year, despite an increase in pupil numbers.
- All schools have a School Travel Plan:
  - Collaborates with the Council to reduce car travel and encourage public transport.
  - Contact your school to learn about their initiatives for sustainable and safe travel.

**Flu: The Facts**

**A**

- Flu (influenza) is an acute viral respiratory infection.
- It spreads easily from person to person at home, school, work, supermarkets, or on public transport.

**B**

- Flu is transmitted through:
  - Airborne droplets from coughs or sneezes.
  - Hands infected by the virus.

**C**

- Symptoms include:
  - Fever, chills, headache, muscle pain, extreme fatigue.
  - Dry cough, sore throat, and stuffy nose.
- Most people recover within a week, but flu can cause severe illness or death in high-risk individuals.
- Annually, 18,500-24,800 deaths in England and Wales are attributed to influenza infections.

**D**

- Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent flu.
- High-risk groups include:
  - People over 65 years old.
  - Those with asthma, diabetes, or certain other conditions.
  - Pregnant individuals and carers.
- High-risk groups are eligible for a free flu vaccination.

**E**

- If not eligible for a free vaccination, you can get vaccinated at a local pharmacy.

**F**

- After vaccination:
  - Your body makes antibodies within 7-10 days to protect against similar viruses.
  - Protection lasts about a year.

**G**

- Flu vaccinations contain inactivated, killed virus strains, so they cannot give you the flu.
- It takes up to two weeks for the vaccine to work, so it is possible to catch flu during this period.

**H**

- Flu vaccinations protect against the most common and potent strains of flu.
- There is a small chance of catching a strain not included in the vaccine.

**I**

- The influenza virus changes constantly.
- Vaccines are updated annually to protect against predicted strains.
- It is important to get vaccinated against the latest strains.

Speak to your GP or nurse today to book your flu vaccination.

title: Business Presentations & Journalism Jobs
passageText:
**Tips for Giving an Effective Business Presentation**

**Preparation**

- Get someone else to evaluate your performance and highlight your best skills.
  - For example, go through your presentation in front of a colleague or relative.
- Think about:
  - Who your audience is.
  - What you want them to get out of the presentation.
  - Content and style.
- Try out any moves you may have to make in the presentation room, such as:
  - Getting up from your chair.
  - Moving to the podium.
- Familiarise yourself with the electronic equipment before the presentation.
- Have a backup plan for unexpected problems, like a power cut.

**Dealing with Presentation Nervousness**

- A certain amount of nervousness is vital for a good presentation.
  - Adrenaline keeps your faculties sharp and gives extra force to your presentation skills.
- To manage tension in the upper chest:
  - Concentrate on your breathing and slow it down to relax.
- Having something to pick up and put down can help.
- Engage in a displacement activity (e.g., clicking a pen, fiddling with jewellery) to feel more secure at the start.
  - A limited amount of this will not be too obvious.

**Interacting with Your Audience**

- Think of your presentation as a conversation with your audience.
  - Make them feel consulted, questioned, and challenged to keep them attentive.
- Engage with your present audience, not the one you prepared for.
- Look for reactions to your ideas and respond to them.
  - If your audience doesn’t appear to follow, find another way to get your ideas across.
- Interaction is key; otherwise, you might as well send a video recording instead.

**Structuring Effective Presentations**

- Use plenty of examples to help your listeners understand your points.
  - Examples make your presentation quicker and more colourful.
- Stick to three or four main ideas.
- For subsidiary information that cannot fit into 20 minutes, use another medium, such as handouts.
- End confidently, even if you feel the presentation didn’t go well.
  - A good finish will get you applause — and you deserve it!

**How to Get a Job in Journalism**

- Employers value practical knowledge over theoretical qualifications.
  - Create real stories with strict deadlines.
  - Write for your school magazine and try editing.
- Request internships in local newspapers.
  - These are generally short-term and unpaid but teach essential skills like:
    - Laying out articles.
    - Creating web pages.
    - Taking good digital pictures.
- Keep a copy of every story you’ve had published (cuttings).
  - Start creating a portfolio to showcase your developing talent.
  - Impressive cuttings can be the deciding factor in getting a job.
- Research thoroughly before applying for a job.
  - Helps decide if the job is right for you.
  - Impress editors by knowing a lot about their paper.
- Perfect your CV:
  - Keep it brief (no more than one page).
  - Ensure accuracy (no spelling or typing errors).
  - Maintain clarity (easy to follow).
- Write an appropriate covering letter:
  - Convey your love of journalism and eagerness to work.
  - Ensure the style is professional and suitable for journalism.

title: Running a large supermarket
passageText:
**What Is It Like to Run a Large Supermarket?**

Jill Insley finds out.

**A**

- Good service is key to improving the shopping experience.
- The Thamesmead branch of Morrisons follows the maxim: help, offer, thank.
  - Identify customers who might need help.
  - Greet them, ask what they need, provide it, thank them, and leave them in peace.
  - Customers who don’t look like they want help are left alone.
- Staff are expected to be friendly to everyone.
  - Checkout assistants aim to amuse and engage customers.
- Adrian Perriss, the branch manager, ensures staff understand the approach.
  - He believes in recognising when someone needs help without being a nuisance.

**B**

- The store opens at 7 am, Monday to Saturday.
  - Some staff, including Perriss, arrive at 6 am to prepare for the morning rush.
- Overnight activities include:
  - 20 people unloading three enormous trailers full of groceries.
  - Ensuring the store is clean, safe, and stocked.

**C**

- Perriss started working in supermarkets in 1982 as a trolley boy.
  - Weekly salary: £76.
  - Roles included trolleys, portering, bread, cakes, dairy, and general maintenance.
- Career progression:
  - Produce department → Produce manager → Assistant store manager → Store manager (1998).
  - Underwent intensive training through the company’s future store manager programme.
  - First store as manager closed soon after (not his fault).

**D**

- Perriss’s career advanced despite the initial setback.
- Managed the launch of new stores and a ‘concept’ store.
  - Introduced ideas like in-store pizza preparation, florists, and fruit/vegetable markets.
  - Hosted all Morrisons’ managers for three days to showcase the concept.
- The role involved long hours and hard work.

**E**

- Perriss’s job has a practical aspect.
  - He chats with staff while checking counters and produce quality.
  - Rejects substandard items, such as split or green potatoes and squashy lemons.
- Weekly wastage is minimal:
  - £4,200 worth of produce is marked down for quick sale.
  - Only £400 worth is scrapped.
- Morrisons uses manual ordering instead of computers.
  - Department heads predict sales based on records and factors like weather.

**F**

- Perriss oversees 1,000 man-hours a week across the store.
- He has a key team of four responsible for different departments.
- Encourages staff development:
  - Held a ‘talent’ day for employees interested in promotions.
  - Twenty-three employees discussed progression and how to become supervisors.

**G**

- Perriss’s favourite department is fish.
  - The 4 m-long counter is run by Debbie and Angela, who engage with customers.
- Managing all 20+ departments is challenging.
  - Daily pressure to ensure everything runs smoothly.
  - Perriss minimises issues and keeps perspective.
- He loves his job and believes passion is essential for success.

title: Organising a Business Conference & Appraisals
passageText:
**HOW TO ORGANISE A SUCCESSFUL BUSINESS CONFERENCE**

**To start with**

- Advance planning is the key to a hassle-free conference.
- The key players of a successful conference are the delegates, so:
  - Identify the audience.
  - Tailor the programme to their particular needs.

**Where and when**

- Choose the date and venue, which are often interdependent.
- Consider the following when selecting the date:
  - Timing of similar regular events to avoid clashes.
  - Holiday periods when people may be away.
- When choosing a venue, check:
  - Accessibility by train, plane, and availability of parking.
  - Size of the main lecture hall for the anticipated number of delegates.
  - Potential for breakout areas for group discussions.
  - Lounge area for tea/coffee breaks.
  - Exhibition space for display stands if required.

**Who**

- Choose and invite speakers, giving them ample notice.
- Select speakers who are known to speak well.
- Avoid speaking yourself in addition to organising the conference, as it can be too demanding.

**Contacting people**

- Send an early mailshot to inform people of the date and venue.
  - This allows interested individuals to mark their diaries.
- Contact speakers again to:
  - Confirm their topic.
  - Discuss available audio-visual aids.
  - Find out their accommodation requirements.
  - Request a written summary of their presentation for distribution.

**Final arrangements**

- Confirm provisional numbers with the venue 4-5 weeks before the conference.
- Confirm final numbers, menus, and arrangements 2 weeks prior.
- Prepare delegate packs, including:
  - Name badge.
  - Delegate list.
  - Programme.
- Ensure the venue provides pads of paper and pens.
- Prepare questionnaires for delegates to complete at the end of the conference.
  - Use responses to gauge success and plan the next conference.

**How to deal with the annual performance appraisal**

**Preparation**

- Send your boss a summary of your achievements, including:
  - Activities.
  - Special assignments.
  - Projects you were in charge of.
- Keep regular notes of achievements to make this easier.
- Create a list of questions to discuss during the appraisal, focusing on:
  - Your role in the company.
  - Additional responsibilities you would like.
  - Clarification of priorities.
  - Personal and professional improvements (not financial considerations).

**During the appraisal**

- Present a positive attitude as soon as you enter the room.
- Take negative assessments constructively:
  - Avoid seeing them as personal attacks.
  - Use them to improve your performance.
- A realistic assessment of strengths and weaknesses can help you advance in the company.

**After the appraisal**

- Create a list of personal goals based on the appraisal, ensuring they are:
  - Detailed.
  - Measurable.
- Send the list to your boss to show you took the appraisal seriously.
- Use the list to achieve higher scores in the next appraisal.
- Request a mid-term review 6 months after the appraisal to:
  - Discuss your progress.
  - Get more feedback to improve.
- Regular check-ins with your boss can:
  - Highlight your dedication.
  - Address criticisms before the next formal review.

title: Efforts to save a special bird — the spoon-billed sandpiper
passageText:
**Efforts to save a special bird — the spoon-billed sandpiper**

**Last year an international team of ornithologists devised a bold plan to rescue one of the world’s rarest birds. Gerrit Vyn reports.**

**A**

- At first glance, the spoon-billed sandpiper resembles other small migratory birds of the sandpiper family that breed across the Arctic.
- Unique features:
  - Flattened bill that flares out into a ‘spoon’ at the end.
  - Russian name, kulik-lopaten, means ‘shovel beak’.
  - Bill dimensions: 19 mm long and 10 mm wide near the tip, with sharp serrations called papillae.
- Theories about the bill’s function vary, but comparisons to the spoonbill are misleading.

**B**

- Until recently, the spoon-billed sandpiper had never been fully documented.
- Efforts by ‘Birds Russia’ included:
  - Producing a photographic and audio record of the bird.
  - Organising an international expedition to North-East Russia.
- Primary aim of the expedition:
  - Collect eggs from wild sandpipers.
  - Hatch the eggs in captivity and establish a self-sustaining population at WWT Slimbridge in the UK.
  - Provide a ‘safety net’ against extinction.

**C**

- The sandpipers travel approximately 8,000 km from their wintering grounds in South-East Asia to North-East Russia.
- Reasons for the journey:
  - Relatively few predators in the tundra.
  - Abundance of insects during the Arctic summer creates ideal conditions for raising chicks.

**D**

- Two main factors contributing to the sandpiper’s decline:
  - Destruction of stopover habitats due to industrial development.
  - Hunting on wintering grounds in some Asian countries.
- Conservation efforts include:
  - Providing alternative income sources to hunters, such as cool boxes for selling fish.
  - Encouraging a halt to bird-netting.

**E**

- The expedition team’s observations:
  - First sandpiper spotted after seven days.
  - Nine nests found in total, but one was lost to a predator.
- Egg collection process:
  - 20 eggs collected and incubated.
  - Females likely to lay replacements as it was early in the breeding season.
- Witnessing the chicks hatch:
  - First chicks emerged after 50 days.
  - Observations included their oversized legs and feet and their first calls.
  - Concerns remained about dangers on their migration route and wintering areas.

**F**

- Rescue plan developments:
  - Young chicks flown to WWT Slimbridge.
  - High-tech biosecure unit built to house the birds.
  - Hygiene measures include:
    - Full-body overalls and rubber shoes for staff.
    - Handwashing before entering.
    - Avoiding risks such as human hair harming the chicks.
- Final stage of the rescue plan:
  - Fly eggs back to Russia and release the chicks there.
  - A gamble, but necessary to save the species.

title: Consumer Advice & Rice Cookers
passageText:

- If something you’ve ordered hasn’t arrived, you should contact the seller to find out where it is.

title: Safety when working on roofs & Maternity allowance
passageText:
**Safety when working on roofs**

- A fall from height is the most serious hazard associated with roof work.
- Key facts:
  - More than 50% of falls are from under three metres.
  - Most falls occur from ladders and roofs.
  - Residential building sites have the highest number of injuries in the construction sector.
  - The cost of these falls is estimated at $24 million annually, excluding human costs.

**Preventing injuries:**

- Conduct a hazard assessment for all roof work to identify potential dangers.
  - Assess hazards before work starts.
  - Repeat hazard identification periodically or when conditions change (e.g., weather, staff numbers).
- Eliminate hazards where possible during design, construction planning, and tendering stages.
- If elimination is not possible:
  - Use edge protection, such as existing scaffolding or temporary work platforms.
  - Consider safety nets or similar systems to minimise injury if a fall occurs.
- Ladders:
  - Use only for short-duration maintenance work (e.g., touching up paint).
  - Train workers in ladder selection and safe use.
  - Inspect ladders regularly to ensure safety.

**Maternity allowance for working women**

- Eligibility:
  - You can claim Maternity Allowance after 26 weeks of pregnancy.
  - Payments start 11 weeks before your baby’s due date.
- Amounts:
  - £140.98 a week or 90% of your average weekly earnings (whichever is less) for 39 weeks.
  - £27 a week for 14 weeks.

**Maternity Allowance for 39 weeks:**

- You might qualify if:
  - You’re employed.
  - You’re self-employed and pay Class 2 National Insurance (including voluntary contributions).
  - You’ve recently stopped working.
  - Qualification is possible even with different jobs or periods of unemployment.

**Maternity Allowance for 14 weeks:**

- You might qualify if, for at least 26 weeks in the 66 weeks before your baby is due:
  - You were married or in a civil partnership.
  - You were not employed or self-employed.

title: The California Gold Rush of 1849
passageText:
**The California Gold Rush of 1849**

**A**

- On January 24, 1848, James Wilson Marshall, a carpenter, found small flakes of gold in the American River near Coloma, California.
- Context:
  - Marshall was building a water-powered sawmill for businessman John Sutter.
  - Days after the discovery, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the Mexican-American War, transferring California to the United States.
- Population at the time:
  - 6,500 Californios (people of Spanish or Mexican descent).
  - 700 foreigners (primarily Americans).
  - 150,000 Native Americans.

**B**

- News of the discovery spread despite Marshall and Sutter’s attempts to keep it quiet.
- Key events:
  - By mid-March 1848, newspapers reported large quantities of gold being found.
  - Storekeeper Sam Brannan sparked a frenzy by parading through San Francisco with a bottle of gold from Sutter’s Creek.
  - By mid-June, three-quarters of San Francisco’s male population had left for the gold mines.
  - By August, the number of miners in the area reached 4,000.

**C**

- Early migrants came from nearby regions accessible by boat, such as:
  - Oregon, Hawaii (then the Sandwich Islands), Mexico, Chile, Peru, and China.
- Later migrants came from the East Coast of the United States.
  - Many borrowed money, mortgaged property, or spent life savings to travel to California.
  - Wives took on new responsibilities, such as running farms or businesses, often with great success.
- Population growth:
  - March 1848: 800 non-native residents.
  - End of 1848: 20,000 non-native residents.
  - End of 1849: 100,000 non-native residents.
- Towns sprang up to accommodate miners, with shops and businesses seeking their own fortunes.
- San Francisco developed a bustling economy and became the central metropolis of the new frontier.

**D**

- Gold mining methods:
  - **Panning**:
    - Place gold-bearing materials (e.g., river gravel) in a shallow pan, add water, and swirl.
    - Heavier gold nuggets or dust settled at the bottom.
    - Slow process: one miner could wash about 50 pans in a 12-hour workday.
  - **Rocker**:
    - Introduced by Isaac Humphrey.
    - Rectangular wooden box set at a downward angle and mounted on a rocking mechanism.
    - Process:
      - Dirt and rock dumped into the top, followed by water.
      - Rocker agitated by hand.
      - Big rocks caught in a sieve; waste exited with water; heavy gold fell to the bottom.
    - Advantages:
      - Portable and did not require a constant water source.
      - Processed more dirt and rock than panning.
    - Disadvantages:
      - Difficulty trapping fine gold (‘flour’).
      - Some miners added mercury to trap fine gold, which was later heated to vaporize the mercury and leave gold behind.

**E**

- By 1850, surface gold had largely disappeared, but miners continued to arrive.
- Challenges:
  - Mining was difficult and dangerous.
  - Striking it rich required luck, skill, and hard work.
  - Average daily pay for independent miners dropped sharply after 1848.
- Industrialization of mining:
  - Hydraulic mining, developed in 1853, brought enormous profits but destroyed much of the region’s landscape.

**F**

- Gold mining peaked in 1852, with $81 million worth of gold extracted.
- Decline:
  - Total gold extraction declined gradually after 1852, leveling off at around $45 million per year by 1857.
- Settlement continued:
  - By the end of the 1850s, California’s population reached 380,000.

title: Health and safety for plumbers & Flexible working
passageText:
**Workplace health and safety considerations for plumbers**

- Plumbing can be a dangerous job, so it is important to take all reasonably practicable measures to keep customers and yourself incident and injury-free.

**Biohazard waste**

- Plumbers regularly come into contact with biohazard waste.
- Key facts:
  - Communicable diseases from work-related exposures to biological hazards such as sewage cause an estimated 320,000 deaths globally each year (Safe Work Australia).
  - Other biohazards include mould, bacteria, and algae.
- Safety measures:
  - Use appropriate protective clothing and equipment to minimize risks.

**Confined spaces**

- Risks:
  - Contaminants such as airborne gases, vapours, and dusts may cause injury from fire or explosion.
  - High concentrations of airborne contaminants can harm health.
  - Drowning is a potential hazard if water sources are not adequately cut off.
- Examples:
  - A plumber was fined $220,000 after an employee suffered carbon-monoxide poisoning.
- Guidelines:
  - Follow the Safe Work Australia confined spaces code of practice to avoid illness and injury.

**Electricity**

- Known as ‘plumbing’s hidden killer’ by the Master Plumbers’ Association.
- Risks:
  - Metal pipes are conductive.
- Safety measures:
  - Insulated gloves should be part of a plumber’s tool kit.
    - Check gloves before every use and replace them every 12 to 14 months.
  - Use a plumbing voltage monitor and a volt tester.
  - Regularly check electrical equipment like bridging conductors.
    - Ensure equipment has appropriate tags verifying its safety.
  - Stop the project immediately if there is any sign of electricity.
    - Disconnect power by a qualified electrician before continuing work.

**How to manage flexible working with your employees**

- Flexible working has grown enormously in recent years but requires careful management.

**Key principles:**

- **Trust:**
  - Flexible workers should be trusted and given well-defined objectives.
  - Assess contributions based on output, not time spent on the job.
- **Daily reviews:**
  - Initially, set up an end-of-the-day review to track progress.
  - Gradually reduce this contact as everyone adjusts to the new setup.
- **Shared calendar access:**
  - Ensure everyone has access to a shared calendar to plan meetings and catch-ups.
- **Technology tools:**
  - Use tools like iMeet for remote collaboration.
    - Features include video conferencing, live chat, file sharing, and screen sharing.

**Benefits of flexible working:**

- **For employees:**
  - Increased productivity due to working exact hours and fewer distractions.
  - Enhanced creativity from working outside office confines.
  - Improved motivation from a better work-life balance.
- **For businesses:**
  - Easier recruitment and retention of top talent.
  - A happier workforce leads to greater success.

title: Preventing the theft of turtle eggs
passageText:
**Preventing the theft of turtle eggs**

**A**

- Humans have been eating sea turtle eggs (and killing adult turtles for meat) for millennia.
- Threats to sea turtles:
  - Intensive fishing.
  - Beach development.
  - Climate change.
- Population status:
  - All but one of the world’s seven species of sea turtles are considered threatened (IUCN Red List).
  - The flatback turtle is listed as data deficient, meaning its status is unknown.

**B**

- Poaching:
  - Millions of sea turtle eggs are illegally taken by poachers annually.
  - Nicaragua is home to four sea turtle species and faces severe poaching issues.
- Key facts:
  - Poaching occurs even on well-protected beaches.
  - Poachers dig up nests just meters from tourists.
  - Arribadas (mass nesting events) lead to frenzied poaching.

**C**

- Challenges in stopping poaching:
  - Armed guards are outnumbered by poachers 10 or 20 to one.
  - Arribadas attract gangs of poachers from outside local communities.
- Conservation strategy:
  - Focus on identifying middlemen and higher-level operators in the distribution chain.

**D**

- High-tech solution:
  - Paso Pacifico is creating fake sea turtle eggs with GPS tracking devices.
  - Purpose: To track the destination markets for trafficked eggs.
- Challenges in creating fake eggs:
  - Sea turtle eggs have flexible shells, unlike bird eggs.
  - Special effects artist Lauren Wilde is developing realistic outer shells using land turtle eggs from California.
  - GPS device placement:
    - A 3D-printed plastic ball with a GPS transmitter replaces the embryo inside the shell.
    - The shell is sealed with silicone to make it waterproof.

**E**

- Deployment of fake eggs:
  - Sea turtles lay around 100 eggs per nest.
  - Fake eggs will be slipped into nests with real ones.
  - Poachers often back off when tourists approach, allowing conservationists to place fake eggs.
- Tracking stolen eggs:
  - Conservationists and law enforcement agents can track eggs to their destinations.
  - Suspected routes include El Salvador, Guatemala, and possibly the USA.

**F**

- Current status:
  - No fake eggs have been deployed yet.
  - Poachers are unlikely to detect fake eggs during nighttime poaching.
- Future plans:
  - Deploy a large number of fake eggs to gather data before poachers become aware.
  - Use data to focus conservation and law enforcement efforts on key areas.
  - Share the technology globally to combat sea turtle egg trafficking.

title: How animals keep fit
passageText:
**How Animals Keep Fit**

No one would dream of running a marathon without proper training. Even with preparation, running 42 kilometres is physically demanding. Now consider the barnacle goose, which migrates around 3,000 kilometres every year. Surprisingly, instead of training, these birds mostly sit on water and eat extensively. According to environmental physiologist Lewis Halsey, this behavior is enough to prepare them for the journey.

Until recently, scientists had not seriously questioned whether exercise is as essential to fitness in animals as it is in humans. It has long been assumed that animals stay fit through activities like hunting and escaping predators. However, this assumption may not be entirely accurate.

For example, domestic cats spend much of their time resting rather than being active. Despite this, they can move incredibly fast when necessary. Similarly, black and brown bears maintain their muscle mass even after months of hibernation without physical activity.

Barnacle geese go even further. While resting and feeding, they not only maintain their fitness but also develop stronger hearts and larger flight muscles. This allows them to complete long migrations, sometimes lasting just two days, covering thousands of kilometres.

This raises an important question: if exercise is not the key factor, what drives physical fitness in animals? From a biological perspective, fitness simply means that the body undergoes changes to become stronger and more efficient. In animals like bears, these changes may be triggered by environmental cues such as falling temperatures or limited food supply. During hibernation, these cues lead to the release of compounds that protect muscles from deterioration.

Barnacle geese may also respond to environmental signals, such as temperature changes, which prepare their bodies for upcoming physical challenges. In other bird species, different cues may play a role. For instance, physiological ecologist Chris Guglielmo studied migratory songbirds known as yellow-rumped warblers. By adjusting their exposure to daylight, researchers were able to trigger long-duration flight behavior without prior training. Under the right conditions, these birds could fly for up to 10 hours continuously.

Unlike these animals, humans do not have biological shortcuts to fitness. Instead, human evolution has tightly linked physical fitness to exercise. Our ancestors lived unpredictable lives, requiring both endurance and efficiency. They needed to run long distances to hunt and escape danger, but also conserve energy by minimizing muscle mass, as maintaining muscle requires significant energy.

Each kilogram of muscle consumes approximately 10 to 15 kilocalories per day at rest. Since muscles make up about 40 percent of body mass, this represents a substantial portion of daily energy use. According to evolutionary biologist Daniel Lieberman, humans spend around 20 percent of their basic energy budget maintaining muscle.

As a result, human physiology evolved to allow fitness and body weight to fluctuate based on activity levels and food availability. This makes humans different from most animals, which typically rely on short bursts of intense activity rather than sustained endurance. For example, a cheetah or gazelle depends on speed over short distances, while even domestic cats only need brief moments of activity to stay fit.

Humans, however, evolved for endurance. Lieberman suggests that early humans became highly adapted long-distance runners, capable of pursuing prey over extended periods. However, this ability depends on consistent training. Without it, humans quickly lose fitness.

Finally, unlike humans, most animals do not aim for peak performance. Barnacle geese do not need to break speed records during migration; they only need to reach their destination. Exercise physiologist Ross Tucker notes that humans may be the only species concerned with maximizing performance. Apart from selectively bred animals like racehorses and greyhounds, most animals are not directly competing to improve their physical capabilities. As a result, the role of training in enhancing animal performance remains uncertain.

**New Cycle Path to Marshbrook Country Park**

**A. Route Overview**
A new dual-purpose cycle and pedestrian route has been built from Atherton bus station to the country park’s main entrance at Marshbrook. It avoids the main road into Atherton on the south side and mainly follows quieter roads. Once outside the built-up area, the path continues through the countryside until it reaches Marshbrook.

**B. Funding and Construction**
Funding for the cycle path has come largely from the county and town councils, with nearly one-third raised through crowdfunding. Maintenance of the path is the responsibility of the county council. The project was completed ahead of schedule, partly due to ideal construction weather, and was delivered under budget.

**C. Project Leadership**
Annie Newcome, chief executive of Cycle Atherton, led the initiative to encourage safer and more frequent cycling. The organisation originally proposed the 12-kilometre route and actively promoted it. Ms Newcome expressed great satisfaction that the funding efforts were successful.

**D. Accessibility and Benefits**
Marshbrook Country Park is a highly popular recreational area, and the new path provides an environmentally friendly way to access it. At 2.5 metres wide, the route is suitable for wheelchair users, mobility scooters, and buggies—groups that previously needed motor vehicles to reach the park.

**E. Ongoing Improvements**
Although the path is now open, improvements are still being made. These include better signage, such as warnings near road crossings. Additionally, hedges and trees will be planted along parts of the route to provide wind protection and support local wildlife.

**F. Additional Information**
Further details and a downloadable map of the route, including a proposed 5-kilometre extension, are available online. Visit the county council website and follow the links to Atherton Cycle Path.
